messages.subject: Multivariate Probit (once again)
parts:
Hi,

I apologize to keep asking questions on this particular model, as from reading old posts on the MVP, it seems like maybe the MVP is just generally a tough fit for STAN. However, I thought I'd try one last request to see if anyone out there has come across any tricks for improvement. Like others, I have had trouble getting neff up for lp__ in this model. I have gathered from old posts that it has to do with high correlation in the posterior between the parameters and latent variable. 

The alternative I have is a JAGS version. Aside from a different prior on the correlations, you estimate the covariance, Sigma, using the wishart, and then rescale all of the betas based on the diagonal. Compared to Bob's version in STAN with the LKJ prior on Omega_L, which is the cholesky of the correlation matrix with diagonal 1. Of course, the JAGS version takes at least an order of magnitude longer to run, and neff can also be a little troublesome, though it typically will converge well after enough iterations. Generally, for 5 or less responses, the JAGS thing takes about 20-30 min to do what the STAN version does in 20 seconds to a couple of minutes. So naturally, I want to use STAN! And I generally like the LKJ prior, because it is just more intuitive for me.

However, aside from the general problem with convergence of lp__, which I could live with, the STAN model doesn't seem to do well at recovering Omega, in particular, compared to the JAGS version. I'm not sure if it has to do with the lkj prior (I've tried eta=4, 2, 1.5, and 1 to no avail) or is a symptom of something else, but Omega is very nearly always underestimated, particularly for larger correlations, of course. Basically, it seems harder to pull the correlations away from unit correlation than it should be. The JAGS version seems to do a better job with this. I attached a couple of pictures showing an example comparing a run with JAGS vs STAN with 4 responses and N=100. The fake data was generated with Bob C's sim for mvp. This is just one example, but is representative, though maybe not as bad as many others I've done with larger and smaller D with pretty much the same issues.

Finally, I have also noticed that the STAN version tends to maybe systematically over-/underestimate some betas for some D. Too negative for truly negative betas and too positive to true positive ones. I didn't test this formally, but it seems that placing a strong prior (e.g., normal(0,1) vs. normal(0,5)) on the betas in STAN maybe helps a little with this, which helps maybe a little with Omega. I attached figures for comparison.

So, I guess I'm just throwing out some symptoms in a last ditch effort with hopes someone with more expertise (I'm an ecologist and relatively new bayesian/STAN user) might be able to diagnose a problem for which there is a solution in STAN. I've also attached the two models. Please let me know if there is anything else I could provide that might help.

Thanks for reading.

-Roy


Omega figures: Top figure is STAN, bottom is JAGS





Beta figures (STAN top, JAGS bottom):





STAN model:


 data {
  int<lower=1> K;
 int<lower=1> D;
 int<lower=1> N;
 matrix<lower=-1,upper=1>[N,D] y;
 matrix[N,K] x;
 }
parameters {
 matrix[K,D] beta;
 cholesky_factor_corr[D] L_Omega;
 matrix<lower=0>[N,D] abs_ystar; //latent variable
 }
transformed parameters {
 matrix[N,D] z;
 z <- (y .* abs_ystar);
 }
model {
 L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(1);
 to_vector(beta) ~ normal(0,5);
 { 
  matrix[N,D] beta_x;
  beta_x <- x * beta;
  for (n in 1:N)
   z[n,] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(beta_x[n,], L_Omega);
  }
 }
generated quantities {
 matrix[D,N] z_new;
 matrix[D,D] Omega;
 Omega <- multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L_Omega);
 {
  matrix[D,N] beta_x;
  beta_x <- (x * beta)';
  for (n in 1:N)
   z_new[,n] <- multi_normal_cholesky_rng(beta_x[,n], L_Omega);
  }
 }



JAGS model:

model{
 for(n in 1:N){
  Z[n, 1:D] ~ dmnorm(Mu[n, ], Tau[, ])
 for(d in 1:D){
  Mu[n, d] <- inprod(Beta.raw[d, ], X[n, ])
  y[n, d] ~ dbern(p[n, d])
  p[n, d] <- step(Z[n, d])
  }
 }
 for(d in 1:D){
 for(k in 1:K){
  Beta.raw[d, k] ~ dnorm(0, 0.2)
  }
 }
 Tau[1:D, 1:D] ~ dwish(ID[, ], df)
 }

Hi Andrew,

Thanks for taking the time. You are correct that the models are different in terms of how the latent variable is implemented. Sorry, that is probably confusing. In the STAN version I posted, I used a -1/1 thing for binary y, which I picked up from an earlier post here from I believe K Van Horn. This was slightly different than Bob C's model, which  builds off of 0/1 for y, so I thought I would give KVH's version a shot. All in all, it turned out that the two gave virtually identical answers and the same issues remained with Omega and Beta. The -1/1 thing seemed to work ever so slightly faster, however, so I just left it at that. 

Yep, KVH 's and Bob's latent coding are also different from the BUGS one. I did try to use something similar to that BUGS coding in STAN, but I don't think I quite figured the translation. I posted what I tried below. The model ran but basically gave nonsense answers after a long run, so I'm sure I misinterpreted something there.

I'm not sure I follow your last question precisely, but I did not try simulating from the priors with no data, if that is what you mean. I did, however, run a post-check on z for the STAN model (generated quantities) to compare new z with toy data z, which checked out decent in some cases, but there is an issue there. Almost invariably, for several D (the multivariate binary responses), one or two of the new z's will be slightly off, such that toy z is overestimated at low values and underestimated at high values or the opposite. Some D are right on though. Hopefully that makes some sense. I attached another figure to illustrate. I had to run the model again (on the same toy data) to generate it, so it doesn't perfectly match the run for the other figures, but the point should be clear. 

Thanks again.

When you say the parameters don't fit, the question is
whether 50% of them are in the 50% posterior intervals.
Not whether they're all exactly right. You won't
typically be able to recover fake data exactly perfectly
except in the asymptotic limit of infinite data.

Are the R-hats near 1? Are the effective sample sizes
reasonable?

I take it in those figures that the red circles are
simulated values and the dots are posterior means or
medians and the intervals are some kind of posterior
interval? And what was the eta in the LKJ prior you were
using and how much data was there?

Are you sure JAGS is getting into the tails of this model?
Assuming the intervals are the same quantiles, the posteiror
uncertainty looks larger in the Stna model.

You may want to try writing exactly the same model in
Stan. It's hard to compare apples and oranges.

As to the simulations with higher variance, it will be harder
to fit for the same reason it's always harder to fit if you
simulate with higher variance --- there's more sampling
variation with higher variance, so you need more data to
recover the true values of the other parameters. (Just
think of generating 10 draws with normal(0, 0.1) vs. normal(0, 10).
You'll get averages much closer to 0 with the former than the
latter.

- Bob

Hey Bob (and Andrew),

Many thanks for taking the time again. And sorry for the delayed response. I spent some time head scratching and thinking about your helpful comments and believe I came to a resolution. 

Essentially, I believe I just wasn't considering the scales correctly here. I went back to thinking about Andrew's 2006 paper on weakly informative priors for logistic regression and realized that the betas I was simulating for this probit-based model probably just didn't make any sense! I was thinking about logit scale, when I should have been considering that the scale for probit coefficients should be smaller; about 1.6 times smaller, I gathered from a little googling. 

So, going back to Gelman et al. (2006), I took the recommended weakly informative priors for logit parameters and used that idea to roughly divide everything I was thinking before by 1.6 for the simulation of fake data. I changed the prior in the Stan (not STAN!) model for the betas to Cauchy, following the paper, with scale = 2.5/1.6. As a result, everything is running quite well (and fast!) and parameter recovery, post-checks, etc are all pretty nice. Well, lp_  can still be a little troublesome, but for the most part it converges with relatively low neff (around 10% to 15% of total posterior samples). Varying N also has the expected behavior. Great!

Though it isn't much different from your original sim and model, Bob, I'll post my fake data simulation and Stan model below in case anyone runs across this and finds it useful.

Many thanks again,

-Roy

Fake data simulation
set.seed(6)
N <- 1000
D <- 2
x <- cbind(
  x1=as.numeric(rnorm(N)>0),
  x2=rnorm(N,0,0.5),
  x3=rnorm(N,0,0.5),
  x4=rnorm(N,0,0.5),
  x5=rnorm(N,0,0.5))

K <- ncol(x)
beta <- matrix(rnorm(D * K, 0, 0.9), D, K)

set.seed(6)

# stick breaking construction to generate a random correlation matrix
L_Omega <- matrix(0,D,D);
L_Omega[1,1] <- 1;
for (i in 2:D) {
  bound <- 1;
  for (j in 1:(i-1)) {
    L_Omega[i,j] <- runif(1, -sqrt(bound), sqrt(bound));
    bound <- bound - L_Omega[i,j]^2;
  }
  L_Omega[i,i] <- sqrt(bound);
}

Omega <- L_Omega %*% t(L_Omega);

yMatLin <- (x %*% t(beta))
z <- yMatLin + rmvnorm(N, sigma=Omega)
y <- ifelse(z > 0,1,0)

data {
 int<lower=1> K;
 int<lower=1> D;
 int<lower=1> N;
 matrix<lower=-1,upper=1>[N,D] y;
 matrix[N,K] x;
 }
parameters {
 matrix[K,D] beta;
 cholesky_factor_corr[D] L_Omega;
 matrix<lower=0>[N,D] abs_ystar; //latent variable
 }
transformed parameters {
 matrix[N,D] z;
 z <- (y .* abs_ystar);
 }
model {
 L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(1);

to_vector(beta) ~ cauchy(0, 1.5625);
 {

matrix[N,D] beta_x;
  beta_x <- x * beta;
  for (n in 1:N)
   z[n,] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(beta_x[n,], L_Omega);
  }
 }
generated quantities {
 matrix[D,N] z_new;
 matrix[D,D] Omega;
 Omega <- multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L_Omega);
 {
  matrix[D,N] beta_x;
  beta_x <- (x * beta)';
  for (n in 1:N)
   z_new[,n] <- multi_normal_cholesky_rng(beta_x[,n], L_Omega);
  }
 }

On Saturday, June 4, 2016 at 1:45:30 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
When you say the parameters don't fit, the question is
whether 50% of them are in the 50% posterior intervals.
Not whether they're all exactly right.  You won't
typically be able to recover fake data exactly perfectly
except in the asymptotic limit of infinite data.

Are the R-hats near 1?  Are the effective sample sizes
reasonable?

I take it in those figures that the red circles are
simulated values and the dots are posterior means or
medians and the intervals are some kind of posterior
interval?  And what was the eta in the LKJ prior you were
using and how much data was there?

Are you sure JAGS is getting into the tails of this model?
Assuming the intervals are the same quantiles, the posteiror
uncertainty looks larger in the Stna model.

You may want to try writing exactly the same model in
Stan.  It's hard to compare apples and oranges.

As to the simulations with higher variance, it will be harder
to fit for the same reason it's always harder to fit if you
simulate with higher variance --- there's more sampling
variation with higher variance, so you need more data to
recover the true values of the other parameters.  (Just
think of generating 10 draws with normal(0, 0.1) vs. normal(0, 10).
You'll get averages much closer to 0 with the former than the
latter.

- Bob

P.S.  "Stan" isn't an acronym.

Hi again,

I thought I'd update this thread, as I believe I recently stumbled upon another potential variation of the "Folk Theorem" in this MVP model sim. After much consternation surrounding recovery of Omega (the correlation of D responses) from fake data with larger D (more response vectors), I came to the conclusion that generating Omega by building up the Cholesky, as shown above, perhaps doesn't work that well when D is larger than say, 10 or so. Sorry, I haven't yet fully gathered why that might be and maybe someone could fill me in or just tell me I'm wrong. Maybe it has something to do with this interesting description Ben Goodrich posted way back when: (https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/YlwuJgCmLxk/2VoGOKkfRkIJ), which I haven't yet had the time to contemplate. 

Nevertheless, I was fairly frustrated by this behavior with fake data because the results I've gotten using real ecological data have seemed highly reasonable. So, recently I ran across a script on Richard McElreath's Rethinking Github for generating random correlations from the LKJ distribution. It turned out that using that script to generate the fake Omega for this MVP model produced much nicer results, though lp__ is still shaky in some cases as expected. Yet, in every case I've tried so far (with D up to 30), all parameters fall within credible intervals at roughly the rates expected, with neff > 10%, etc etc. By comparison, with the previous approach to simulating Omega, the modeled 95% intervals would include the simulated Omega values no more than 70% of the time, typically due to drastic underestimates of the absolute magnitude of larger correlations.

So, I thought I'd follow up on this thread with this tidbit above and tack on the code from Rethinking for simulating the correlations, which I believe follows code from Ben Goodrich (according to the Github comments). #Code to generate Omega from the LKJ distribution (from Richard McElreath's Rethinking package)
rlkjcorr <- function ( n , K , eta = 1 ) {
  
  stopifnot(is.numeric(K), K >= 2, K == as.integer(K))
  stopifnot(eta > 0)
  #if (K == 1) return(matrix(1, 1, 1))
  
  f <- function() {
    alpha <- eta + (K - 2)/2
    r12 <- 2 * rbeta(1, alpha, alpha) - 1
    R <- matrix(0, K, K) # upper triangular Cholesky factor until return()
    R[1,1] <- 1
    R[1,2] <- r12
    R[2,2] <- sqrt(1 - r12^2)
    if(K > 2) for (m in 2:(K - 1)) {
      alpha <- alpha - 0.5
      y <- rbeta(1, m / 2, alpha)
      
      # Draw uniformally on a hypersphere
      z <- rnorm(m, 0, 1)
      z <- z / sqrt(crossprod(z)[1])
      
      R[1:m,m+1] <- sqrt(y) * z
      R[m+1,m+1] <- sqrt(1 - y)
    }
    return(crossprod(R))
  }
  R <- replicate( n , f() )
  if ( dim(R)[3]==1 ) {
    R <- R[,,1]
  } else {
    # need to move 3rd dimension to front, so conforms to array structure that Stan uses
    R <- aperm(R,c(3,1,2))
  }
  return(R)
}

Omega <- rlkjcorr(1, D, eta=1)

Thanks for following up. Indeed, you need to simulate
properly from the model if you want to recover parameters
properly.

The LKJ distribution was developed by Ben from
Lewandowski, Kurowicka and Joe's paper on generating
random correlation matrices. There's a duality between
generating random variates and defining a distribution.

I don't know what you mean by building up the Cholesky.
My guess is that you missed the rather involved Jacobian
that we explain in the manual following the LKJ paper.
That's the tricky bit of both random generation and
writing the prior.

You can actually use Stan's generated quantities block
to generate random correlation matrices using
lkj_corr_rng or lkj_cholesky_corr_rng depending on whether
you want the full matrix or the Chokesky factor.

If you use eta = 1, you get uniformly distributed random
correlation matrices. You'll get the same distribution of
random variates using lkj_corr_rng and taking the Cholesky
factor as using lkj_cholesky_corr_rng.

If code's open source, reposting it is legal if it's
accompanied by the license. Usually in these kinds of
situations, people don't mind. You'd need a lawyer and
a court case to sort out fair use in these situations.

Generally, for 5 or less responses, the JAGS thing takes about 20-30 min to do what the STAN version does in 20 seconds to a couple of minutes. So naturally, I want to use STAN! And I generally like the LKJ prior, because it is just more intuitive for me.
> > >
> > > However, aside from the general problem with convergence of lp__, which I could live with, the STAN model doesn't seem to do well at recovering Omega, in particular, compared to the JAGS version. I'm not sure if it has to do with the lkj prior (I've tried eta=4, 2, 1.5, and 1 to no avail) or is a symptom of something else, but Omega is very nearly always underestimated, particularly for larger correlations, of course. Basically, it seems harder to pull the correlations away from unit correlation than it should be. The JAGS version seems to do a better job with this. I attached a couple of pictures showing an example comparing a run with JAGS vs STAN with 4 responses and N=100. The fake data was generated with Bob C's sim for mvp. This is just one example, but is representative, though maybe not as bad as many others I've done with larger and smaller D with pretty much the same issues.
> > >
> > > Finally, I have also noticed that the STAN version tends to maybe systematically over-/underestimate some betas for some D. Too negative for truly negative betas and too positive to true positive ones. I didn't test this formally, but it seems that placing a strong prior (e.g., normal(0,1) vs. normal(0,5)) on the betas in STAN maybe helps a little with this, which helps maybe a little with Omega. I attached figures for comparison.
> > >
> > > So, I guess I'm just throwing out some symptoms in a last ditch effort with hopes someone with more expertise (I'm an ecologist and relatively new bayesian/STAN user) might be able to diagnose a problem for which there is a solution in STAN. I've also attached the two models. Please let me know if there is anything else I could provide that might help.

On Monday, August 15, 2016 at 5:58:14 PM UTC-4, Roy Martin wrote:
I thought I'd update this thread, as I believe I recently stumbled upon another potential variation of the "Folk Theorem" in this MVP model sim. After much consternation surrounding recovery of Omega (the correlation of D responses) from fake data with larger D (more response vectors), I came to the conclusion that generating Omega by building up the Cholesky, as shown above, perhaps doesn't work that well when D is larger than say, 10 or so. Sorry, I haven't yet fully gathered why that might be and maybe someone could fill me in or just tell me I'm wrong. Maybe it has something to do with this interesting description Ben Goodrich posted way back when: (https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/YlwuJgCmLxk/2VoGOKkfRkIJ), which I haven't yet had the time to contemplate.

The onion method is probably more numerically stable than the transformation of canonical partial correlations that is used in Stan, but they yield the same density for correlation matrix. If your problem is lack of numerical stability, then maybe the onion transformation will help. But in a model, you wouldn't use the _rng function; you need to declare the primitives as parameters, do the onion transformation to get the (Cholesky factor of the) correlation matrix, evaluate the likelihood of the data given the (Cholesky factor of the) correlation matrix, and put the corresponding priors on the primitives such that the resulting correlation matrix is distributed LKJ a priori.

Ben
